title: Cao Chong Weighs the Elephant: Did the Story Come From a Buddhist Sutra?
description:
Sun Quan sent a huge elephant. Cao Cao asked all his men how heavy it was and none could say; his young son Cao Chong said: put the elephant on a big boat, mark the waterline, then weigh goods and load them to the same mark. The same puzzle appears in a Buddhist sutra, the Za Baozang Jing, in the story of the Land That Cast Out Its Elders: there it is answered, almost the same way, by an old man hidden in an underground room.

This episode follows the doubts in the order they arose. The passage in the main text of Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms (no year, no stones, no age for Cao Chong that year). Two years set side by side by the Qing scholar He Zhuo: by the Records Cao Chong died in Jian'an 13 (208), a eulogy says Jian'an 12 (207), and Sun Quan took Jiaozhou only in Jian'an 15 (210). Chen Yinke's 1930 article in the Tsinghua Journal and his verdict, and the sutra's translation, made in 472 AD, 175 years after Chen Shou died. Last, the other side: the "two tame elephants" from Sun Quan in Cao Pi's letter to Wang Lang, the tame elephants kept at the Jin court, the Jiangbiao Zhuan's "still young", and the big pig weighed by boat in the Fuzi. This file remains open.

Histories follow the Wenyuange Siku Quanshu Records (with Pei Songzhi's notes and the collation notes) and the Book of Jin. The lost Jiangbiao Zhuan, letter to Wang Lang, Fuzi, eulogy for Cao Chong and Jin Zhugong Zan are read as quoted in the Yiwen Leiju, Chuxue Ji and Taiping Yulan; the sutra in CBETA's Taishō edition (T0203) and the Chu Sanzang Jiji; Chen Yinke's article in a scan of the Tsinghua Journal 6.1 (June 1930), pp. 17-20, whose contents page says "Indian tales" where its heading says "Buddhist tales". Sources for every quotation, year and number are in the references below; sentences beginning "we think" are this channel's view. This episode is about where texts came from and comments on no faith.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses.

Information as of 2026-10-19

cc101.text: In the Jian'an years, Sun Quan sent a huge elephant.

cc102.text: Cao Cao wanted its weight. None of his men could say.

cc103.text: His young son Cao Chong said:

cc104.text: put it on a boat, mark the water;

cc105.text: then weigh goods and load them until they reach the mark.

cc106.text: The same puzzle is in a sutra.

cc107.text: An old man answers it, hiding in an underground room.

cc109.text: He too says: boat, mark the water.

cc111.text: A Qing scholar ran the numbers on this elephant.

cc112.text: Someone else found a pig put on a boat.

cc113.text: In 1930, someone opened that sutra and passed a verdict.

cc114.text: And a letter mentions two tame elephants. Who wrote it?

cc115.text: Marking water on a boat: who really thought of it first?

cc201.text: Cao Chong's tale is in Chen Shou's main text, not a later note.

cc202.text: Chen Shou died in 297 AD; the book was done before that.

cc203.text: He opens the elephant with one word, shi: "at that time."

cc204.text: What year? Sent where? He doesn't say.

cc205.text: And how old was Cao Chong?

cc206.text: Chen Shou says he was bright; at five or six, wise as an adult.

cc207.text: The elephant comes right after, but no age is given.

cc208.text: The familiar "weighed it at five or six" is a later reading.

cc209.text: And in "weigh goods and load them", he never says what goods.

cc210.text: In the version you know, was it stones?

cc211.text: Pei Songzhi, who later annotated the book, put no note here; no sign of doubt.

cc212.text: But the year Cao Chong died, Chen Shou states clearly. Which?

cc301.text: Jian'an 13, 208 AD: Cao Chong fell ill. He was thirteen.

cc302.text: Cao Cao prayed for him himself, but could not save him.

cc303.text: Another text mourning him gives a year earlier: Jian'an 12.

cc304.text: By the Records, that year Sun Quan and Liu Bei beat Cao Cao at Red Cliffs.

cc305.text: Open war began; Sun Quan submitted nine years later.

cc306.text: So when did Sun Quan send the elephant?

cc307.text: That Qing scholar with the numbers was He Zhuo. He found two years.

cc308.text: In 200 AD, Sun Ce died; Sun Quan had just taken over.

cc309.text: In 210 AD, Sun Quan sent a governor; only then did Jiaozhou submit.

cc311.text: He Zhuo: once he held Jiaozhou, Sun Quan could send one, but Cao Chong was long dead.

cc312.text: So, he said, the story was embellished.

cc313.text: Odder still: in the whole Records, notes included, Sun Quan sends Cao Cao an elephant only here.

cc314.text: Another Qing scholar, Shao Jinhan, found that pig.

cc315.text: It's in an old book called Fuzi.

cc316.text: A king got a huge pig; it broke ten scale beams.

cc317.text: At last his water official weighed it by boat: 1,000 jun.

cc318.text: Shao Jinhan said weighing by boat existed long before Cao Chong.

cc320.text: The book itself is lost; we couldn't verify its date;

cc321.text: and it only says "by boat", not how to mark it or what to load.

cc322.text: But if the story was embellished, where did the method come from?

cc401.text: That 1930 scholar, Chen Yinke, said: from a Buddhist sutra.

cc402.text: He said He Zhuo and Shao Jinhan missed it.

cc403.text: It ran in that June's Tsinghua Journal; its title links Cao Chong to Buddhist tales.

cc404.text: The sutra: Za Baozang Jing. One story: the Land That Cast Out Elders.

cc406.text: That was his country: by its law, all old people were sent far away.

cc407.text: His son, a minister, couldn't bear it, so he hid and cared for him.

cc408.text: Then a god set nine riddles.

cc409.text: The first two: tell a snake's sex, and who's asleep or awake.

cc410.text: Weighing the elephant was third; no minister knew how.

cc411.text: The minister went home to ask his father. Did he say more this time?

cc412.text: He added two things: put the boat in a big pond;

cc413.text: load that boat with stones to the line: that's the weight.

cc414.text: The stones Chen Shou left out are in the sutra.

cc415.text: All nine solved, the king ruled: no more exiling elders; care for them.

cc416.text: The story ends: that old father was the Buddha in a past life.

cc417.text: It's about honoring elders, not wit.

cc418.text: How did a tale about elders become Cao Chong's?

cc419.text: Chen Yinke: elephants are southern, none in Cao Cao's lands, so Sun Quan had to send it.

cc420.text: His verdict: Cao Chong's tale took in a Buddhist story;

cc421.text: even an eye like Chen Shou's couldn't tell.

cc422.text: But when was this sutra translated into Chinese?

cc423.text: In 472 AD, under the Northern Wei, by two monks.

cc424.text: Remember when Chen Shou died? This translation came 175 years after him.

cc425.text: Chen Yinke's answer: it was compiled from other sutras,

cc426.text: many of its stories appear in other translations.

cc427.text: So this one may have had an earlier, lost translation; or it reached China by word of mouth and was pinned on Cao Chong.

cc428.text: But he could not show a single earlier translation.

cc429.text: Could no elephant reach Cao Cao's lands?

cc501.text: Someone had to send an elephant; and while Cao Chong lived, Jiangdong sent tribute to the Han court.

cc503.text: and from 196 AD, that court was in Cao Cao's hands.

cc504.text: So the tribute really went to Cao Cao.

cc505.text: But both were wary: in 202 AD, Cao Cao asked Sun Quan for a son as hostage, and Sun Quan refused.

cc506.text: An elephant as goodwill: plausible, and not.

cc507.text: Yet no record from those years mentions an elephant.

cc508.text: So did any record say Sun Quan sent an elephant north?

cc509.text: In 219 AD, Sun Quan wrote to Cao Cao, submitting as a vassal.

cc510.text: Later, that letter from the start appears: Cao Pi wrote it, to Wang Lang.

cc511.text: It says Sun Quan again sent envoys to submit, with two tame elephants, a male and a female.

cc512.text: It gives no year. All that's sure: Cao Chong had been dead over ten years.

cc513.text: Compendia say Sun Quan gave Liu Shan of Shu two tame elephants.

cc514.text: Nor was that the last: the Jin court kept tame elephants sent from the south.

cc515.text: It had a cart, ridden by Nanyue men; each New Year audience, it was led into the hall.

cc516.text: So we think Chen Yinke's claim went too far.

cc517.text: Who besides Chen Shou wrote about weighing the elephant?

cc518.text: We said the Records has only that passage; but another Jin book tells it too.

cc519.text: That book says Sun Quan sent two tame elephants, and Cao Chong was "still young."

cc520.text: The age Chen Shou left out still has no number here.

cc521.text: Did one copy the other, or share a source?

cc523.text: What's sure: before that sutra's translation, two Jin writers recorded it.

cc524.text: Scholars today both back and refute Chen Yinke.

cc525.text: Remember? Who first thought of marking water,

cc526.text: no document can say for sure.

cc527.text: We think the same idea landed on a child in the histories, and on an old man in the sutra.

cc529.text: First heard it in a textbook, storybook or cartoon?

cc530.text: We tell only what the records hold. Subscribe to open the files with us.
